scenario.title: Meeting Summary and Email Reporting
scenario.initial_description: After a meeting, the contents are summarized and shared by email with the relevant people.

reference_workflow.goal: Summarize meeting content and distribute decisions, owners, and deadlines to relevant stakeholders.

activities.name: Confirm unclear items with decision owners

decisions.condition: Are all action items assigned to owners?
Does the meeting require task tracking?

automation_opportunities.rationale: Decision and action-item extraction can be supported by summarization models.
Task tracker updates can be generated from action-item tables.

activities.name: Compose Summary Email
outputs: Drafted summary email with attachment or inline content

activities.name: Archive Meeting Summary
activities.system: Document management system or shared drive

decisions.condition: Is the draft meeting summary accurate and complete?
branches: Yes: Proceed to identify distribution list
No: Return to note taker for revision and re-drafting

decisions.condition: Are there additional stakeholders beyond meeting attendees who should receive the summary?
branches: Yes: Expand distribution list to include additional stakeholders
No: Use attendee list as distribution list

decisions.condition: Does the summary contain sensitive or confidential information?
branches: Yes: Apply access restrictions, limit distribution, or seek approval before sending

exceptions: Meeting notes are incomplete or missing due to note taker absence
Key decisions or action items are disputed by participants
Distribution list is incorrect or outdated, causing misdirected emails
Email delivery failure for one or more recipients
Summary contains confidential content shared inadvertently with wrong audience
Meeting recording or transcript is unavailable for reference during summarization
Delay in approval causes summary to be sent long after the meeting

dependencies.condition: No sensitive content or approval obtained

automation_opportunities.rationale: AI-powered transcription tools can automatically capture spoken content during meetings in real time, reducing reliance on manual note taking and improving accuracy and completeness.
constraints: Participant consent required for recording
Audio quality must be sufficient
Multi-language meetings may reduce transcription accuracy

automation_opportunities.rationale: Large language models can automatically generate structured summaries from transcripts or raw notes, identifying key decisions, action items, and discussion points with minimal manual effort.
constraints: Output quality depends on transcript quality
Sensitive topics may require human oversight before distribution
Model must be configured for organizational tone and format

automation_opportunities.target: D1 - Is the draft meeting summary accurate and complete?
automation_opportunities.rationale: Automated quality checks can flag incomplete summaries, missing action item owners, or absent decision records before routing for human review, reducing revision cycles.
constraints: Rules for completeness must be predefined
Subjective accuracy still requires human judgment

automation_opportunities.rationale: Distribution lists can be automatically derived from meeting calendar invites, role-based rules, or project membership data, reducing manual lookup effort and errors.
constraints: Stakeholder registry must be current and accessible
Edge cases such as external guests may require manual verification

automation_opportunities.rationale: Email composition can be fully automated using predefined templates populated with the approved summary, action items, and distribution list, eliminating manual formatting effort.
required_data: Meeting metadata such as date and title
constraints: Template must be maintained and version-controlled
Personalization requirements may limit full automation

automation_opportunities.rationale: Automated email dispatch can be triggered immediately upon summary approval, ensuring timely delivery without manual intervention and enabling delivery tracking.
constraints: Email system integration required
Sensitive content classification must be resolved before automated sending
Approval gate must be enforced programmatically

automation_opportunities.rationale: Archiving can be automated upon email send confirmation, storing the summary in a predefined location with standardized naming and tagging for future retrieval.
constraints: Folder structure and naming conventions must be standardized
Access control policies must be applied automatically

automation_opportunities.target: D3 - Does the summary contain sensitive or confidential information?
automation_opportunities.rationale: Automated content classification can scan summaries for sensitive keywords, data categories, or named entities and flag them before distribution, reducing risk of inadvertent disclosure.
constraints: Classification rules must be maintained and updated
False positives may create unnecessary delays
Final determination may still require human review

assumptions: Meetings are scheduled through a calendar system that contains attendee and agenda information.
A designated note taker or meeting organizer is always present or assigned.
The organization has access to or can adopt AI transcription or summarization tooling.
An email system is available and accessible programmatically for automated dispatch.
A document management system or shared drive exists for archiving purposes.
Participant consent for recording is either already in place or can be established.
The frequency of meetings is regular enough to justify automation investment.
Meeting summaries follow a consistent structure including decisions, action items, and next steps.
Distribution lists can be partially or fully derived from structured data sources such as calendar invites or project registries.
Sensitive content classification is a recognized concern and some governance rules exist or can be defined.

missing_information.gap: No information on who is responsible for creating the meeting summary (e.g., meeting host, designated note-taker, rotating role, or an automated transcription tool).
missing_information.why_it_matters: Identifying the actor determines whether summarization is a manual human task or already partially automated, directly affecting automation potential.

missing_information.gap: No details on the source material for the summary (e.g., handwritten notes, audio recording, video recording, chat transcript, shared document during meeting).
missing_information.why_it_matters: The input format determines which automation tools (e.g., speech-to-text, AI summarization) are applicable and what integration is needed.

missing_information.gap: No information on the meeting platform used (e.g., video conferencing, in-person, phone), nor the email system used for distribution.
missing_information.why_it_matters: System identification is essential to assess API availability, integration feasibility, and whether native automation hooks exist.

missing_information.gap: No criteria defined for determining who the 'relevant people' are for email distribution (e.g., attendees only, additional stakeholders, management escalation).
missing_information.why_it_matters: Without a clear rule for recipient selection, the distribution step cannot be automated reliably and may require manual judgment each time.

missing_information.gap: No standard format or template specified for the meeting summary (e.g., bullet points, action items section, decisions log, structured template).
missing_information.why_it_matters: A lack of output standardization means automation cannot reliably generate or validate the summary content before sending.

missing_information.gap: No information on how often meetings occur, the volume of summaries produced per week or month, or whether meeting types vary (e.g., recurring vs. ad hoc).
missing_information.why_it_matters: Frequency and volume data are critical for estimating automation ROI and prioritizing implementation effort.

missing_information.gap: No estimate of the time spent per meeting on summarization and email preparation, nor the total effort across the organization.
missing_information.why_it_matters: Without effort estimates, it is impossible to quantify the automation benefit or build a business case.

missing_information.gap: No information on exception cases such as confidential meetings, partially attended meetings, meetings with no clear outcomes, or failed email delivery.
missing_information.why_it_matters: Unhandled exceptions can cause automation failures or data governance violations if sensitive content is distributed incorrectly.

missing_information.gap: No details on whether action items from the summary feed into downstream systems (e.g., task management, CRM, project tracking tools).
missing_information.why_it_matters: If summaries trigger downstream workflows, a broader automation scope may be needed and integration dependencies must be mapped.

missing_information.gap: No clarity on whether meeting recordings or transcripts are currently stored and accessible in a structured, retrievable format.
missing_information.why_it_matters: Automation of summarization depends on having reliable, machine-readable input data; unavailability blocks AI-assisted approaches.

clarification_questions.question: Who currently creates the meeting summary, and what source material do they use (e.g., personal notes, recording, transcript)?
Which platform is used to host meetings, and which email system is used to distribute the summary?
How is the list of email recipients determined after each meeting — is it always the attendees, or does someone manually curate the distribution list?
Is there a standard template or required structure for the meeting summary (e.g., attendees, decisions, action items, deadlines), or does the format vary?
Approximately how many meetings per week require a summary and email, and how much time on average does the full process take per meeting?
Are there any meetings considered confidential or sensitive where the normal summarization and distribution process should not apply, and if so, how are these currently handled?
